y-m-46-01.title: 서윤's distance calculation: where did it go wrong?
y-m-46-01.topic: The distance between two parallel lines
y-m-46-01.goal: Find and fix the line where a solution for the distance between two parallel lines written with different coefficients goes wrong, and make two lines that fit a condition.
y-m-46-01.material: 서윤 solved as below to find the distance between the two lines l: 2x + y − 3 = 0 and m: 4x + 2y + 5 = 0. (2x + y − 3 = 0 is read 'two x plus y minus three equals zero'. √5 is read 'root five'.) The two lines are parallel to each other. In the solution below, each line has a number.
y-m-46-01.thinking.0: Finding the error line by line in a solution
y-m-46-01.thinking.1: Checking why you must match the coefficients before comparing
y-m-46-01.thinking.2: Making many lines that satisfy a condition
y-m-46-01.prereq.0: School-order assumption: assume the learner has already studied 'equations of figures' in high school Common Mathematics (equations of lines and circles and the distance between a point and a line). H3 is a difficulty level of this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum places this content in a particular grade.
y-m-46-01.prereq.1: The form ax+by+c=0 of the equation of a line, and judging parallel lines by slope
y-m-46-01.prereq.2: How to find the distance between a point and a line (high school Common Mathematics, equations of figures)
y-m-46-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in 서윤's solution that is wrong.
y-m-46-01.s.s1.hint.0: Write the coefficients of x and y of the two equations side by side and compare whether they have the same form.
y-m-46-01.s.s1.line.0: l: 2x + y − 3 = 0 and m: 4x + 2y + 5 = 0 have the same ratio of the coefficients of x and y, 2 : 1 = 4 : 2, so they are parallel.
y-m-46-01.s.s1.line.1: The distance between two parallel lines with the same coefficients ax + by + c₁ = 0, ax + by + c₂ = 0 is |c₁ − c₂| ÷ √(a² + b²).
y-m-46-01.s.s1.line.2: The constant term of l is −3 and that of m is 5, so the difference of the constant terms is |5 − (−3)| = 8.
y-m-46-01.s.s1.line.3: Using the coefficients of l, √(2² + 1²) = √5, so the distance is 8 ÷ √5 = 8√5/5.
y-m-46-01.s.s1.explain: Line 3 goes wrong. The method in line 2 can be used only when the coefficients of x and y in the two equations are exactly the same, but l has 2x + y and m has 4x + 2y, so the coefficients differ. Yet in line 3 the constant terms −3 and 5 were subtracted as they are, without matching the coefficients. Line 4 inherited that value. If you divide m by 2 to match it as 2x + y + 5/2 = 0, the difference of the constant terms is |5/2 − (−3)| = 11/2 and the distance is (11/2) ÷ √5 = 11√5/10.
y-m-46-01.s.s2.prompt: When 서윤's solution is corrected, which is the right distance between the two lines l and m?
y-m-46-01.s.s2.hint.0: Find a point on l that is easy to calculate with (for example, when x = 0).
y-m-46-01.s.s2.hint.1: Find the distance from that point to m and compare it with the values in the choices.
y-m-46-01.s.s2.r.a: This is 서윤's value as it is. It is the value that used the difference of the constant terms with the coefficients different.
y-m-46-01.s.s2.r.b: It used 8 as the difference of the constant terms, without matching the coefficients, and changed the denominator to the coefficients of m. The standards in the two places are different.
y-m-46-01.s.s2.r.c: It matched the difference of the constant terms, 11, but used the coefficients of l (√5) in the denominator. The difference of the constant terms of the form 4x + 2y and √(4² + 2²) must be taken from the same equation.
y-m-46-01.s.s2.r.d: After matching the coefficients of the two lines to be the same, it took the difference of the constant terms and the denominator from the same equation.
y-m-46-01.s.s2.explain: Measuring directly the distance from the point (0, 3) on l to m also gives |0 + 6 + 5| ÷ √(16 + 4) = 11/(2√5) = 11√5/10. The method of matching coefficients and the method of measuring from one point give the same value.
y-m-46-01.s.s3.prompt: Make two lines 2x + y + k = 0 that are parallel to l and at distance exactly √5 from l, with two different values of k.
y-m-46-01.s.s3.hint.0: A line parallel to l has the same coefficients of x and y and differs only in the constant term. Change the constant term a few times and test the distance.
y-m-46-01.s.s3.hint.1: If you found one, think about whether there is a line at the same distance on the opposite side of l.
y-m-46-01.s.s3.ok.c1: It is a line different from l.
y-m-46-01.s.s3.fail.c1: If k = −3, it is the same line as l, so the distance is 0.
y-m-46-01.s.s3.fail.c2: The distance to l is not √5. Since the coefficients are the same, look at the difference of the constant terms divided by √5.
y-m-46-01.s.s3.explain: If k = 2, the difference of the constant terms is |2 − (−3)| = 5 and 5/√5 = √5, and if k = −8, |−8 − (−3)| = 5, so it is likewise √5. There is one on each side of l.
y-m-46-01.s.s1.hint.1: For each line, write down the condition of the method used in the previous line (what form it must have to be usable), and check one by one whether that line kept that condition.

y-m-46-02.title: A circle through two points: what else must we know to determine it uniquely?
y-m-46-02.topic: The center and radius of a circle through two points
y-m-46-02.goal: Make circles through two points yourself to confirm there are many, and judge which extra conditions determine the circle uniquely (or fail to, or make it not exist at all).
y-m-46-02.material: On a coordinate plane there are two points A(0, 0), B(0, 8). Think about circles that pass through both A and B. The center of the circle is (a, b) and the radius is r (r > 0). A circle passing through a point means that the distance from that point to the center is r. (A is read 'A' and B is read 'B'.)
y-m-46-02.thinking.0: Judging whether the conditions are enough
y-m-46-02.thinking.2: Designing your own extra condition and giving a reason
y-m-46-02.prereq.0: School-order assumption: assume the learner has already studied 'equations of figures' in high school Common Mathematics (equations of lines and circles and the distance between a point and a line). H3 is a difficulty level of this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum places this content in a particular grade.
y-m-46-02.prereq.1: The equation of a circle (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r² and the meaning of center and radius
y-m-46-02.prereq.2: Writing the distance between two points with coordinates
y-m-46-02.s.s1.hint.0: The center must be the same distance from A and B. Plot two or three candidate centers and look at which line they lie on.
y-m-46-02.s.s1.fail.c1: The radius must be greater than 0.
y-m-46-02.s.s1.fail.c2: The distance from the center (a, b) to A(0, 0) is not r.
y-m-46-02.s.s1.fail.c3: The distance from the center (a, b) to B(0, 8) is not r.
y-m-46-02.s.s1.explain: In all three examples b is 4. This is because points at the same distance from A and B lie on the line y = 4. You can choose a freely, and r² = a² + 16 is determined.
y-m-46-02.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the conditions that, when one is added to the circles through A and B, determine exactly one circle.
y-m-46-02.s.s2.hint.1: First sort out which conditions give two solutions or none at all.
y-m-46-02.s.s2.r.a: With radius 5 the center can be at two places, (3, 4) and (−3, 4). Even though a condition was added, count how many candidates remain.
y-m-46-02.s.s2.o.b: The center is on the line y = x
y-m-46-02.s.s2.r.b: This is the method of seeing how many candidates remain when you use together the fact that the center is on y = 4 and the condition that it is on y = x.
y-m-46-02.s.s2.o.c: The center is on the x-axis
y-m-46-02.s.s2.r.c: The center must be on y = 4, but that never meets the x-axis (y = 0). Having more conditions does not mean a circle exists. There is no such circle at all.
y-m-46-02.s.s2.r.d: This is the method of working out with an equation whether the condition of passing through one more point determines a as one value.
y-m-46-02.s.s2.o.e: It is tangent to the x-axis
y-m-46-02.s.s2.r.e: This is the method of seeing whether the tangency condition becomes an equation between r and b that determines a.
y-m-46-02.s.s2.explain: The center has the form (a, 4) and r² = a² + 16. If it is on y = x then a = 4 (one), if it passes through the point (6, 4) then from a² + 16 = (6 − a)² we get a = 5/3 (one), and if it is tangent to the x-axis then r = 4 so a = 0 (one). If the radius is 5 there are two, a = ±3, and if the center is on the x-axis it contradicts b = 4, so there is no circle.
y-m-46-02.s.s3.prompt: Write an extra condition of your own that makes the circle through A and B determined as exactly one. Also explain how that condition connects with the y-coordinate of the center so that the circle is determined uniquely.
y-m-46-02.s.s3.hint.0: Write what y-coordinate the center of a circle through A and B has.
y-m-46-02.s.s3.hint.1: Count how many values of a come out from the condition you made.
y-m-46-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check with an equation that the condition you made determines a as one value?
y-m-46-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check that your condition is not a case with two circles or none?
y-m-46-02.s.s3.model.0: Extra condition: the radius is 4. The center is the same distance from A and B, so its y-coordinate is 4 and it has the form (a, 4). Putting r = 4 into r² = a² + 16 gives only a = 0, so the circle is determined as exactly one.
y-m-46-02.s.s3.model.1: Add the condition that the center is on the line x = 2. The y-coordinate of the center is already fixed as 4 because of A and B, and the x-coordinate is fixed as 2, so the center (2, 4) is determined uniquely and the circle is one too.
y-m-46-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: A condition made with the position of the center rather than the radius.
y-m-46-02.s.s1.prompt: Make three circles that pass through both A and B, each with a different center. Enter the center (a, b) and the radius r. If the radius is irrational, you may enter a decimal approximation.
y-m-46-02.s.s1.hint.1: Fix the x-coordinate a of the center to an easy value such as 0 or 3, and find b and r that satisfy both conditions for A and B. If r is irrational, you may approximate it with a decimal.
y-m-46-02.s.s2.hint.0: Using the rule for the position of the center that you found in s1, set up an expression in a for each condition and count how many solutions there are.

y-m-46-03.title: If the intercept is greater than the radius, do they not meet?
y-m-46-03.topic: The positions of a circle and a line (number of intersection points)
y-m-46-03.goal: At first estimate the number of intersection points of a slanted line and a circle by the intercept, then find that comparing the distance from the center to the line with the radius is the right criterion, and find the range of k.
y-m-46-03.material: The circle C: x² + y² = 8 has its center at the origin (0, 0) and radius √8, about 2.83. The line l: y = x + k has slope 1 and meets the y-axis at (0, k). Change the value of k and look at how many intersection points C and l have. (x² is read 'x squared', and √8 is read 'root eight'.) The information is revealed one piece at a time, and each time you choose the most fitting judgment now.
y-m-46-03.thinking.0: Revising a judgment when the information grows
y-m-46-03.thinking.1: Sorting out which two quantities to compare
y-m-46-03.thinking.2: Generalizing the range of a parameter
y-m-46-03.prereq.0: School-order assumption: assume the learner has already studied 'equations of figures' in high school Common Mathematics (equations of lines and circles and the distance between a point and a line). H3 is a difficulty level of this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum places this content in a particular grade.
y-m-46-03.prereq.1: The equation of a circle x² + y² = r²
y-m-46-03.prereq.2: How to find the distance between a point and a line
y-m-46-03.s.s1.prompt: Each time information is revealed, choose a judgment about the number of intersection points of C and l.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, tell apart the quantities you know now from the quantities you do not yet know.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.hint.1: Compare with numbers which is larger, the distance from the center to the line or the radius.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.0.info: When k = 3: the line y = x + 3 meets the y-axis at (0, 3). (0, 3) is at distance 3 from the origin, which is farther than the radius of about 2.83. We have not yet calculated the coordinates of the intersection points or the distance from the center to the line.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: With the information we have now, what is the most fitting judgment about the number of intersection points of C and l?
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.0.after: It is true that (0, 3) is outside the circle, but that is just one point of the line. A slanted line can pass through the inside of the circle regardless of its y-intercept, so the number of intersection points is decided by comparing 'the distance from the center to the line' with the radius.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It seems to be 0. The point where the line meets the y-axis is outside the circle.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: One point of the line being outside the circle does not mean the whole line is outside the circle. A slanted line can pass through the inside of the circle on the other side.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It seems to be 2. A line with slope 1 seems to pass close to the circle.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is an estimate that also takes the direction of the line into account. It is good if you know that to settle it you have to measure the distance.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: We cannot decide now. We need to know the distance from the center to the line.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You pointed out what is unknown. This is a judgment that knows which quantity is needed.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It seems to be 1. 3 and 2.83 are almost equal.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.0.r.d: The intercept and the radius being similar does not mean it is tangent. Think about what distance relation the tangency condition is.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.1.info: Information added: the distance from the origin to the line x − y + 3 = 0 is 3/√2 ≈ 2.12. The radius is √8 ≈ 2.83.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now how many intersection points do C and l have?
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.1.after: The distance of about 2.12 is less than the radius of about 2.83, so the line passes through the inside of the circle and meets it at two different points. Even though at first the intercept 3 was greater than the radius, the result is 2.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: 0. The distance from the center to the line is not 0, so they do not meet.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: The distance not being 0 only means the line does not pass through the center. You have to compare the size of the distance with the radius.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 1. If there is a distance, the line is tangent to the circle.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: It is tangent when the distance is exactly equal to the radius. Compare the sizes of 2.12 and 2.83.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: 2. The distance 2.12 is less than the radius 2.83.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: If the distance is less than the radius, the line passes through the inside of the circle. This comparison is the basis of the judgment.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.1.o.d: We still cannot tell. We need to find the coordinates of the intersection points.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Even without finding the coordinates of the intersection points, the number is determined just by comparing the distance and the radius.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.2.info: Change k to 4 so that y = x + 4. The distance from the origin to the line x − y + 4 = 0 is 4/√2. The radius is √8.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: This time how many intersection points are there?
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.2.after: 4/√2 = 4√2/2 = 2√2 and √8 = 2√2, so the distance and the radius are exactly equal. The line is tangent to the circle and there is 1 intersection point.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: 0. 4 is greater than 2.83, so the line is outside the circle.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: 4 is the y-intercept, not the distance from the center to the line. What should be compared is 4/√2 and √8.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You did not look only at decimals but simplified the radicals and confirmed they are the same number. If the distance and the radius are the same, it is tangent.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: 2. Both are about 2.83, so it passes close by.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Even if the approximate decimals are similar, the number differs depending on whether they are exactly equal or which one is smaller.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.2.o.d: We cannot tell. They are similar as decimals, so we cannot distinguish them.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: If you simplify with radicals instead of decimals, you can tell whether the two numbers are equal.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.3.info: k may also be negative. Looking at the distance found so far, the distance from the origin to the line x − y + k = 0 can be written as |k|/√2.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.3.ask: What is the range of k for which the line y = x + k meets C at two different points?
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.3.after: |k|/√2 < 2√2 ⇔ |k| < 4, so there are 2 intersection points when −4 < k < 4, 1 (tangent) when k = ±4, and 0 when |k| > 4.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.3.r.a: This is the range from comparing k directly with the radius √8. What should be compared is not k but |k|/√2.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.3.r.b: You left out the case where k is negative. The case where the line passes the circle from below is also decided in the same way by the distance.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.3.r.c: When k is a very small negative number, the line moves away from the circle. Look at both ends.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.3.r.d: From |k|/√2 < √8 you got |k| < 4. You included both positive and negative values.
y-m-46-03.s.s1.reflect: At first you may have wanted to compare the y-intercept 3 with the radius 2.83. Look back at what the two values to compare changed into as the information grew, and which was the standard at k = 4: the intercept 4 or the distance 4/√2.
y-m-46-03.s.s2.prompt: If you had a first thought when k = 3, write how it changed (or whether it stayed the same), and which two values you must compare to decide the number of intersection points.
y-m-46-03.s.s2.hint.0: Think about which getting larger, the distance or the radius, makes the number of meeting points decrease.
y-m-46-03.s.s2.hint.1: Substitute the numbers for k = 3 and k = 4 one at a time and put them into the sentence.
y-m-46-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: If your first thought changed, did you write what changed it, and if it stayed the same, what evidence you had?
y-m-46-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you sort out how many points there are when the distance or the radius is larger?
y-m-46-03.s.s2.model.0: At first I thought they would not meet because the y-intercept 3 is greater than the radius 2.83, but the distance from the center to the line was 2.12, less than the radius, so there were 2. The number of intersection points is decided not by the intercept but by comparing the distance from the center to the line with the radius.
y-m-46-03.s.s2.model.1: From the start I thought I did not know exactly, and after calculating the distance I settled on 2. If the distance is less than the radius there are 2, if equal it is tangent so 1, and if greater 0, so k is not what is compared.
y-m-46-03.s.s2.modelNote.1: The case of a student who held off from the start
y-m-46-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: 1 point. If you simplify the two values with radicals and compare them exactly, they are equal.

y-m-46-04.title: Do the points whose distances are in the ratio 1 : 2 lie on a line?
y-m-46-04.topic: The locus of points whose ratio of distances is constant
y-m-46-04.material:
On a coordinate plane there are two points A(−2, 0), B(4, 0), and a point P satisfies PB = 2 × PA. (PA is the distance from point P to A.) 민호 said: "If PA = PB, then P is on the perpendicular bisector (a line) of segment AB. When the ratio is 1 : 2, those P will also be on one line." To check 민호's statement, four points satisfying PB = 2 PA were investigated.
Point | PA | PB | PB = 2PA
P1(0, 0) | 2 | 4 | satisfied
P2(−8, 0) | 6 | 12 | satisfied
P3(−4, 4) | √20 | √80 | satisfied
P4(−4, −4) | √20 | √80 | satisfied
(√20 is read 'root twenty'.)
y-m-46-04.thinking.2: Constructing points that satisfy the condition yourself
y-m-46-04.prereq.0: School-order assumption: assume the learner has already studied 'equations of figures' in high school Common Mathematics (equations of lines and circles and the distance between a point and a line). H3 is a difficulty level of this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum places this content in a particular grade.
y-m-46-04.prereq.1: Writing the distance between two points with coordinates
y-m-46-04.prereq.2: Equations of lines and circles and expanding expressions
y-m-46-04.s.s1.prompt: From the four points in the table, what can we say for sure about 민호's statement?
y-m-46-04.s.s1.hint.0: Roughly plot the four points of the table on the coordinate plane and compare where they lie.
y-m-46-04.s.s1.hint.1: Compare slopes to see whether the three points P1, P2, P3 could be on one line.
y-m-46-04.s.s1.o.d: There are only four points, so we cannot say anything about whether 민호's statement is right or wrong.
y-m-46-04.s.s1.r.d: It is hard to settle that it is right, but that it is wrong can be sorted out with one counterexample.
y-m-46-04.s.s1.explain: P1 and P2 are on the x-axis and P3 is not on the x-axis, so the four points are not on one line. These points are all actual points satisfying the condition, so the statement 'every P is on one line' is wrong. However, with only these four points you cannot settle 'the locus is a circle'.
y-m-46-04.s.s2.ok.c2: It is a point not in the table.
y-m-46-04.s.s2.explain: (−1.6, 3.2), (−6.4, −3.2), (−0.8, 2.4) all satisfy PB = 2PA. It is good if you noticed that these points and the four points of the table are all on the circle with center (−4, 0) and radius 4.
y-m-46-04.s.s3.prompt: The points you found all seem to be on the same circle. Then may we conclude that 'the set of all points P satisfying PB = 2PA is that circle'? Write whether we may or not, and what more must be done to settle the conclusion.
y-m-46-04.s.s3.hint.0: Think about which points the points written in the table can represent.
y-m-46-04.s.s3.hint.1: Think about what you would see if you put P as (x, y) and wrote the condition as an equation.
y-m-46-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the checking method I wrote cover both directions: 'every point on this circle satisfies the condition' and 'every point satisfying the condition is on this circle'?
y-m-46-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain in your own words why it cannot be settled with a few points?
y-m-46-04.s.s3.model.0: It cannot be settled yet. A few points being on one circle does not guarantee that all points satisfying the condition are on that circle. We have to put P(x, y), square both sides of PB = 2PA, expand and simplify, and check whether the resulting equation is the equation of a circle.
y-m-46-04.s.s3.model.1: There are only a few points, so it is too early to settle. For all points P we have to write PB² = 4PA² as an equation in x, y and simplify it to see whether it becomes (x + 4)² + y² = 16, and conversely check whether every point on this circle satisfies the condition.
y-m-46-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: A model answer that mentions both directions
y-m-46-04.goal: Distinguish how far you can go with the evidence of a few points, find more points that satisfy the condition to estimate the shape of the locus, and state the procedure needed to confirm it.
y-m-46-04.s.s1.o.a: All four points satisfy the condition, so Minho is right.
y-m-46-04.s.s1.r.a: That there are points satisfying the condition is different from those points being on one line. Compare the positions of the four points.
y-m-46-04.s.s1.o.b: The shape drawn by the four points is a circle, so the locus is a circle.
y-m-46-04.s.s1.r.b: Even if the four points are on one circle, it is not guaranteed that all points satisfying the condition are on that circle.
y-m-46-04.s.s1.o.c: The four points are not on one line, so Minho's statement does not hold.
y-m-46-04.s.s1.r.c: That the actual points satisfying the condition are not on one line is a counterexample.
y-m-46-04.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter 3 different points P(x, y) that satisfy PB = 2 PA and are not in the table. (You may write coordinates to one decimal place. We accept it if the difference between PB and 2PA is within 0.25 because of rounding.)

y-m-46-05.title: Lines through the point (2, 3): which have integer intercepts?
y-m-46-05.topic: Intercepts of a line through one point and the area of a triangle
y-m-46-05.goal: Find all lines through one point whose intercepts are positive integers, and judge whether a few rows of a table are enough to settle 'the minimum of the area'.
y-m-46-05.material:
Consider lines that pass through the point P(2, 3) and meet the positive parts of the x-axis and y-axis. If the x-intercept is a and the y-intercept is b (a > 0, b > 0), the line is x/a + y/b = 1, and since it passes through P, 2/a + 3/b = 1, which simplifies to 3a + 2b = ab. The area of the triangle enclosed by the line and the two axes is ab/2. 서연 investigated a few lines and made a table.
a | b | Area
3 | 9 | 13.5
4 | 6 | 12
5 | 5 | 12.5
6 | 4.5 | 13.5
8 | 4 | 16
서연 said, "Looking at the table, the area can't be less than 12."
y-m-46-05.thinking.0: Making many lines that satisfy a condition
y-m-46-05.thinking.1: Judging how far the evidence in a table goes
y-m-46-05.thinking.2: Describing the limits of a sample
y-m-46-05.prereq.0: School-order assumption: assume the learner has already studied 'equations of figures' in high school Common Mathematics (equations of lines and circles and the distance between a point and a line). y-m-46-05.prereq.1: The equation of a line written with the x-intercept and y-intercept, x/a + y/b = 1

y-m-46-05.s.s1.prompt: Which is the most fitting judgment of 서연's statement?
y-m-46-05.s.s1.hint.0: Think about whether the values in the table represent all the lines.
y-m-46-05.s.s1.hint.1: Pick an a that is not in the table, find b, and find the area directly.
y-m-46-05.s.s1.o.a: All five lines give 12 or more, so we may conclude that all lines give 12 or more.
y-m-46-05.s.s1.r.a: The five lines in the table are not all the possible lines. You have to test whether it is the same for lines not in the table.
y-m-46-05.s.s1.o.b: In the table it is 12 or more, but we should test more lines outside the table.
y-m-46-05.s.s1.r.b: This is the attitude of considering whether a tendency obtained from a sample can be extended beyond the table.
y-m-46-05.s.s1.o.c: The areas vary, so we cannot state a rule that it is 12 or more.
y-m-46-05.s.s1.r.c: Even if the values vary, it is a fact that they are all 12 or more. The question is how far that fact can be trusted.
y-m-46-05.s.s1.o.d: There is a line with area 12, so there must also be a line with area less than 12.
y-m-46-05.s.s1.r.d: The fact that 12 is the smallest in the table does not lead to the conclusion that a smaller value exists.
y-m-46-05.s.s1.explain: The five lines in the table are all 12 or more, but the table is only a part of the possible lines. The table alone does not guarantee that 12 is the minimum among all lines, and you have to test further whether something less than 12 comes out, or work it out with an equation.
y-m-46-05.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different lines through the point P(2, 3) whose x-intercept a and y-intercept b are both positive integers.
y-m-46-05.s.s2.hint.0: Put a value of a into the equation 3a + 2b = ab, find b, and check whether b is also an integer.
y-m-46-05.s.s2.hint.1: Test what happens to the equation if a is 2 or less.

y-m-46-05.s.s3.prompt: Compare the areas of the lines you found in s2. What is the smallest area among them, and can you say that value is the minimum among all lines through the point P? Write it with your reason.
y-m-46-05.s.s3.hint.0: Find the area of each line as ab/2 and write them side by side.
y-m-46-05.s.s3.hint.1: Find which of the conditions of s2 does not apply to all lines.

y-m-46-06.title: Lines tangent to a circle tangent to both axes: make them yourself
y-m-46-06.topic: The condition for a line to be tangent to a circle
y-m-46-06.goal: State the condition for a line to be tangent to a circle in two ways, and make several tangent lines to a given circle yourself and explain the method.
y-m-46-06.material: The circle C: (x − 2)² + (y − 2)² = 4 has center (2, 2) and radius 2. It is tangent to the x-axis at (2, 0) and to the y-axis at (0, 2). For positive p, q, consider the line l: x/p + y/q = 1 with x-intercept p and y-intercept q (which simplifies to qx + py − pq = 0). Look at what relation the triangle enclosed by this line and the two coordinate axes has with C. ((x − 2)² is read 'x minus 2, squared'.)
y-m-46-06.thinking.1: Constructing examples that satisfy the condition yourself
y-m-46-06.prereq.0: School-order assumption: assume the learner has already studied 'equations of figures' in high school Common Mathematics (equations of lines and circles and the distance between a point and a line). H3 is a difficulty level of this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum places this content in a particular grade.
y-m-46-06.prereq.1: The equation of a circle and its center and radius
y-m-46-06.prereq.2: The distance between a point and a line, or the discriminant of a quadratic equation
y-m-46-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the fitting ways to confirm that the line l is tangent to the circle C.
y-m-46-06.s.s1.hint.0: Picture the ways a line can meet a circle one by one and count the intersection points.
y-m-46-06.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what happens between the center and the line when there is exactly one intersection point.
y-m-46-06.s.s1.o.a: The discriminant of the quadratic equation obtained by combining l and C is 0
y-m-46-06.s.s1.r.a: If the combined equation has a double root, there is one intersection point, so it is tangent. This method gives the same conclusion as the distance method.
y-m-46-06.s.s1.o.b: The equation combining l and C has a real root
y-m-46-06.s.s1.r.b: Having a real root means there is at least one intersection point. It includes the case of two intersection points, so it differs from the tangency condition.
y-m-46-06.s.s1.o.c: l passes through the center (2, 2) of the circle
y-m-46-06.s.s1.r.c: A line through the center meets the circle at two points. A tangent line does not pass through the center.
y-m-46-06.s.s1.o.d: The distance from the center (2, 2) to l equals the radius 2
y-m-46-06.s.s1.r.d: This is the method of comparing the distance from the center to the line with the radius.
y-m-46-06.s.s1.explain: Being tangent means there is exactly one intersection point, so either the discriminant of the combined equation is 0 or the distance from the center to the line equals the radius. The two methods give the same result. Having a real root alone can also mean two intersection points.
y-m-46-06.s.s2.prompt: Make two different (p, q) so that the line l with x-intercept p and y-intercept q is tangent to the circle C. (p, q are positive)
y-m-46-06.s.s2.hint.0: Fix one p and change q, testing for the value where the distance from the center to the line is 2.
y-m-46-06.s.s2.hint.1: Another way is to first think of a (p, q) for which the three sides of the triangle are integers.
y-m-46-06.s.s2.fail.c1: p and q must be positive.
y-m-46-06.s.s2.ok.c2: The distance from the center to l is 2.
y-m-46-06.s.s2.fail.c2: The distance from the center (2, 2) to the line qx + py − pq = 0 is not 2. It is not tangent.
y-m-46-06.s.s2.explain: If (p, q) = (6, 8), the line is 8x + 6y − 48 = 0 and the distance to the center is |16 + 12 − 48| ÷ 10 = 2. For (5, 12) it is |24 + 10 − 60| ÷ 13 = 2. Swapping p and q, like (12, 5), (8, 6), gives examples of the same form.
y-m-46-06.s.s3.prompt: Write the process of confirming in one way that the line is tangent to the circle C when (p, q) = (6, 8), and also write in one or two sentences how you found a new (p, q).
y-m-46-06.s.s3.hint.0: Rewrite the equation of the line in the form qx + py − pq = 0.
y-m-46-06.s.s3.hint.1: Write what value the distance from the center to the line must equal when it is tangent.
y-m-46-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the method I chose connect exactly to the tangency condition?
y-m-46-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write the values you tested and their results when finding a new (p, q)?
y-m-46-06.s.s3.model.0: The distance from the center (2, 2) to the line 8x + 6y − 48 = 0 is |16 + 12 − 48| ÷ √(64 + 36) = 20 ÷ 10 = 2, which equals the radius, so it is tangent. For the new pair, I fixed p as 5, looked for the q that gives tangency, and got q = 12.
y-m-46-06.s.s3.model.1: Substituting y = 8 − 4x/3 from the line 8x + 6y = 48 into the equation of the circle gives (25/9)x² − 20x + 36 = 0, and the discriminant is 400 − 400 = 0, so it has a double root and is tangent. The radius is 2, so I checked the 5-12-13 triangle in the same way.

y-m-46-07.title: Can we trust a maximum obtained by testing only integer points?
y-m-46-07.topic: The maximum of a linear expression over a region
y-m-46-07.goal: Find the problem in a solution that got a maximum by checking only integer points, make points in the region that give a larger value yourself, and judge the correct value of the maximum.
y-m-46-07.material: The region D: x² + y² ≤ 4 is the circle with center at the origin and radius 2, together with its inside. 태민 wanted to find the largest value of x + y among the points (x, y) in D, so he collected and checked only the points where x and y are integers. Below is 태민's solution. (x² + y² ≤ 4 is read 'x squared plus y squared is less than or equal to 4'.)
y-m-46-07.thinking.0: Finding the error of generalizing in a solution
y-m-46-07.thinking.2: Judging the candidate for the maximum by distance
y-m-46-07.prereq.0: School-order assumption: assume the learner has already studied 'equations of figures' in high school Common Mathematics (equations of lines and circles and the distance between a point and a line). H3 is a difficulty level of this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum places this content in a particular grade.
y-m-46-07.prereq.1: The region shown by the inequality of a circle x² + y² ≤ r² (the circle and its inside)
y-m-46-07.prereq.2: How to find the distance between a point and a line
y-m-46-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose the line in 태민's solution that is wrong.
y-m-46-07.s.s1.hint.0: Think about whether the points 태민 handled are all the points in D.
y-m-46-07.s.s1.hint.1: For each line, mark whether it is 'about integer points' or 'about all of D'.
y-m-46-07.s.s1.line.1: Among these, the points with the largest x + y are (2, 0), (0, 2), (1, 1), and the value is 2 for all of them.
y-m-46-07.s.s1.line.2: (1, 2) and (2, 1) have x² + y² = 5 > 4, so they are points outside D.
y-m-46-07.s.s1.line.3: Therefore the maximum of x + y in D is 2.
y-m-46-07.s.s1.explain: Line 4 is wrong. Lines 1 to 3 are right when you look only at integer points. But D also has points that are not integers, and line 4 extended the result for integer points to all of D. For example, (1.4, 1.4) has 1.96 + 1.96 = 3.92 ≤ 4, so it is a point in D, and x + y = 2.8 > 2.
y-m-46-07.s.s2.prompt: Make two different points (x, y) in D with x + y > 2. (Decimals may be used)
y-m-46-07.s.s2.hint.0: Pick non-integer values (x, y) and first calculate x² + y² to check that it is at most 4.
y-m-46-07.s.s2.hint.1: Compare how x + y changes when x and y are the same value and when they are different values.
y-m-46-07.s.s2.fail.c1: The point is outside D. Check whether x² + y² is at most 4.
y-m-46-07.s.s2.fail.c2: x + y is at most 2. You need to find a point that goes beyond 태민's maximum of 2.
y-m-46-07.s.s2.explain: (1.4, 1.4) gives x + y = 2.8, and (1.5, 1.2) has x² + y² = 3.69 ≤ 4 and x + y = 2.7. Both are greater than 2, showing that 태민's maximum is wrong.
y-m-46-07.s.s3.prompt: What is the fitting value for the largest value x + y can take in D?
y-m-46-07.s.s3.hint.0: x + y = k are lines with slope −1. Think about the position of the last line that meets D as you increase k.
y-m-46-07.s.s3.hint.1: Express the positional relation of that last line and the circle using the distance from the center.
y-m-46-07.s.s3.r.a: This is the k for which, viewing x + y = k as a tangent line, the distance from the center equals the radius. That value occurs at the point (√2, √2) of D.
y-m-46-07.s.s3.r.b: This is 태민's value from looking at integer points only. You have already confirmed that a larger value came out at non-integer points.
y-m-46-07.s.s3.r.c: √6 is about 2.45. Compare whether the x + y values of the points you made in the earlier step have already exceeded it.
y-m-46-07.s.s3.r.d: The line x + y = 3 is 3/√2 ≈ 2.12 away from the origin, which is farther than the radius 2, so it does not meet D.
y-m-46-07.s.s3.explain: For x + y = k to meet D, the distance from the origin |k|/√2 must be at most 2, so k ≤ 2√2. The maximum is 2√2 ≈ 2.83, attained at the point (√2, √2). The true maximum lies between 태민's value of 2 and the 2.8 of the non-integer point (1.4, 1.4).

y-m-46-08.title: 서아's message: correcting the method for finding a symmetric point
y-m-46-08.topic: Reflection of a point across a line
y-m-46-08.goal: State what the conditions for a symmetric point across a line must be, and write a correction message that refutes with numbers a point obtained by a wrong method, so that a friend can understand it.
y-m-46-08.material: 서아 posted in the group chat the point she got by reflecting the point P(3, 1) across the line y = x. (y = x is read 'y equals x'.) Each line has a number.
y-m-46-08.thinking.0: Telling necessary and sufficient conditions apart
y-m-46-08.thinking.2: Turning it into a text that explains to a friend
y-m-46-08.prereq.0: School-order assumption: assume the learner has already studied 'equations of figures' in high school Common Mathematics (equations of lines and circles and the distance between a point and a line). H3 is a difficulty level of this production assignment and does not mean the curriculum places this content in a particular grade.
y-m-46-08.prereq.1: The midpoint of two points and the condition for two lines to be perpendicular (product of slopes)
y-m-46-08.prereq.2: The line y = x and the coordinates of a point
y-m-46-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in 서아's message that is wrong.
y-m-46-08.s.s1.hint.0: Check whether the conditions 서아 wrote are lacking something needed to say that two points are symmetric about the line.
y-m-46-08.s.s1.hint.1: From P′(−3, −1), find the slope of PP′ and compare it with the slope of y = x.
y-m-46-08.s.s1.line.0: Let P′ be the point obtained by reflecting the point P(3, 1) across the line y = x.
y-m-46-08.s.s1.line.1: For P′ to be the symmetric point of P, it is enough that the midpoint of segment PP′ is on the line y = x.
y-m-46-08.s.s1.line.2: So if we take P′(−3, −1) as a candidate, the midpoint of PP′ is (0, 0).
y-m-46-08.s.s1.line.3: (0, 0) is a point on y = x, so the condition is satisfied.
y-m-46-08.s.s1.line.4: Therefore the reflected point is P′(−3, −1).
y-m-46-08.s.s1.explain: The 'it is enough' in line 2 is the problem. The midpoint being on the line is necessary but not sufficient. The condition that segment PP′ is perpendicular to the line y = x is also needed. The calculations in lines 3 and 4 are right, but the conditions are insufficient, so the conclusion in line 5 is wrong. The slope of the line joining (−3, −1) and P(3, 1) is 1/3, so its product with the slope 1 of y = x is not −1.
y-m-46-08.s.s2.prompt: What is a sufficient check to pick out the symmetric point P′ of the point P(3, 1) across the line y = x?
y-m-46-08.s.s2.hint.0: For the condition in each choice, find a point that satisfies it but is not the symmetric point.
y-m-46-08.s.s2.o.d: The line PP′ is perpendicular to the line y = x (the product of the slopes is −1)
y-m-46-08.s.s2.r.d: There are infinitely many points on a perpendicular line. For example, (4, 0) also satisfies this condition.
y-m-46-08.s.s3.prompt: Write a correction message to send to 서아 in 3 to 5 sentences. It should include the condition missing from 서아's method, why (−3, −1) is not the answer (with numbers), and the correct point and how to check it. Write it so that 서아 can follow it herself.
y-m-46-08.s.s3.hint.0: Think about how it would be to first point out the part 서아 has already done right.
y-m-46-08.s.s3.hint.1: Calculate the slope of the segment joining P(3, 1) and (−3, −1) and put it in the sentence.
y-m-46-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Can 서아 check for herself that (−3, −1) is wrong just by reading this text?
y-m-46-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is the tone one of checking together rather than blaming?
y-m-46-08.s.s3.model.0: 서아, the midpoint being on y = x is not enough by itself. You also need to check the condition that segment PP′ is perpendicular to y = x. If you join (−3, −1) and P(3, 1), the slope is 1/3, so its product with the slope 1 of y = x is not −1, which means it is not perpendicular. The correct point is (1, 3), and its midpoint (2, 2) is on y = x and the slope is −1, so both conditions are met.
y-m-46-08.s.s3.model.1: The problem is that you only looked at the midpoint being on the line. (−3, −1) is the point symmetric to P about the origin, so the midpoint of PP′ is (0, 0), but the slope of PP′ is 1/3, so it is not perpendicular to y = x. If you use the perpendicular condition too, you get (1, 3), with midpoint (2, 2) and slope −1, so both the midpoint condition and the perpendicular condition are met.
y-m-46-08.s.s3.modelNote.1: A model answer that adds the reason of symmetry about the origin
y-m-46-08.s.s2.hint.1: Check one by one whether Sua's candidate (−3, −1) passes the condition of each choice.
y-m-46-08.s.s2.o.a: The midpoint of segment PP′ is on the line y = x
y-m-46-08.s.s2.r.a: (−3, −1), which satisfies only this condition, was Sua's candidate. One more condition is needed.
y-m-46-08.s.s2.o.b: P and P′ are at equal distances from the line y = x, and the midpoint is on y = x
y-m-46-08.s.s2.r.b: Sua's candidate (−3, −1) also has the same distance to the line as P, and its midpoint is on y = x. Check whether there are points that are not filtered out even when both conditions are used together.
y-m-46-08.s.s2.o.c: The midpoint is on y = x and PP′ is perpendicular to y = x
y-m-46-08.s.s2.r.c: If the midpoint condition and the perpendicular condition are used together, the point is determined uniquely.
y-m-46-08.s.s2.explain: If the midpoint is on the line and PP′ is perpendicular to the line, P′ is determined uniquely and is (1, 3). The midpoint (2, 2) is on y = x, and the slope of PP′ is (3 − 1)/(1 − 3) = −1, so its product with the slope 1 of y = x is −1. There are many points that satisfy only the equal distance together with the midpoint being on y = x, only the midpoint being on y = x, or only perpendicularity.

y-m-46-09.title: If the diagonals are perpendicular, is it a rhombus?
y-m-46-09.topic: Judging the shape of a quadrilateral using coordinates
y-m-46-09.goal: Confirm with coordinates that the information that the diagonals are perpendicular is not enough to say it is a rhombus, sort out what more information is needed to be a rhombus, and make a rhombus yourself.
y-m-46-09.material: On a coordinate plane there are four points A(0, 0), B(3, 2), C(0, 8), D(−1, 2). Quadrilateral ABCD connects A, B, C, D in that order. Diagonal AC is on the y-axis and diagonal BD is on the line y = 2, so the two diagonals are perpendicular. 하은 said, "The two diagonals are perpendicular, so ABCD is a rhombus!"
y-m-46-09.thinking.0: Finding a counterexample to a claim
y-m-46-09.thinking.1: Judging whether extra information is enough
y-m-46-09.thinking.2: Constructing a figure that fits the conditions yourself

y-m-46-09.prereq.1: The distance between two points and the coordinates of the midpoint
y-m-46-09.s.s1.prompt: Which judgment about 하은's statement is right?
y-m-46-09.s.s1.hint.0: Find the squares of the lengths of the four sides using coordinates and write them side by side.
y-m-46-09.s.s1.hint.1: Also compare whether the midpoints of the two diagonals are the same point.
y-m-46-09.s.s1.o.a: It is a rhombus. If the diagonals are perpendicular, all four sides are equal in length.

y-m-46-09.s.s1.r.b: All the coordinates are given, so you can find the side lengths directly. This is not a situation where the information is insufficient and cannot be decided.
y-m-46-09.s.s1.o.c: It is not a rhombus. The lengths of sides AB and DA are different.

y-m-46-09.s.s1.explain: AB² = 3² + 2² = 13, BC² = 3² + 6² = 45, CD² = 1² + 6² = 37, DA² = 1² + 2² = 5, so the side lengths are all different. Even if the diagonals are perpendicular, there are quadrilaterals that are not rhombuses.

y-m-46-09.s.s2.r.a: The ratio of the diagonal lengths has no direct relation to whether the four sides are equal. There is a kite shape that satisfies this condition but is not a rhombus.
y-m-46-09.s.s2.o.b: The two diagonals meet at each other's midpoints
y-m-46-09.s.s2.r.b: If the diagonals bisect each other it is a parallelogram, and you can think about what quadrilateral it becomes when perpendicularity is added.
y-m-46-09.s.s2.o.c: The midpoint of diagonal BD is on diagonal AC
y-m-46-09.s.s2.r.c: This condition also holds for a kite shape. The midpoint being on a diagonal is different from the diagonals bisecting each other.
y-m-46-09.s.s2.o.d: All four sides are equal in length
y-m-46-09.s.s2.r.d: This is just the definition of a rhombus. Think about whether it overlaps with information you already have.

y-m-46-09.s.s2.explain: Two diagonals meeting at each other's midpoints make a parallelogram, and adding perpendicularity makes two adjacent sides equal in length, so it becomes a rhombus. If all four sides are equal in length, it is a rhombus by definition. The remaining conditions are all satisfied by kite shapes (not rhombuses) such as A(0, 0), B(2, 2), C(0, 8), D(−2, 2), so they do not guarantee the conclusion.

y-m-46-10.goal: Test with several cases how the order affects the result when a translation and a reflection in the line y = x are done one after the other, find the condition under which the result is the same even if the order is changed, and explain why.
y-m-46-10.material: Circle C: (x − 1)² + (y − 2)² = 4 has center (1, 2) and radius 2. Consider two moves. T(a, b): translate every point by a in the x direction and by b in the y direction. S: reflect in the line y = x. (A point (p, q) is moved to (q, p).) "T then S" means doing T first and then S on the result, and "S then T" means doing S first and then T on the result. A circle keeps its radius when moved, so you only need to follow the position of the center. ((x − 1)² is read "x minus 1, squared," and y = x is read "y equals x.")
y-m-46-10.s.s1.st.0.info: We tried T(3, 3). "T then S": center (1, 2) → (4, 5) → (5, 4). "S then T": center (1, 2) → (2, 1) → (5, 4). The results of the two orders were the same.
y-m-46-10.s.s1.st.0.after: For T(3, 3), the results of the two orders were the same. But there is only one case, so we cannot tell whether this is also true for other T.
y-m-46-10.s.s1.st.0.o.a: If the order is changed, the result is always different.
y-m-46-10.s.s1.st.0.r.a: In the case you just saw, they were the same. This claim does not match the case.
y-m-46-10.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Whatever move T is, the results of the two orders are always the same.
y-m-46-10.s.s1.st.0.r.b: There is only one case. You cannot conclude "always" from one case. You need to test other T as well.
y-m-46-10.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It is a circle, so it is the same regardless of the order.
y-m-46-10.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You should follow where the center goes, not the shape of the circle.
y-m-46-10.s.s1.st.0.o.d: They are the same in this case. We need to test more to know whether they are the same for other T as well.
y-m-46-10.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This is an attitude of considering whether something that was the same in one case can be extended to the general case.
y-m-46-10.s.s1.st.1.info: We tried T(3, 0). "T then S": center (1, 2) → (4, 2) → (2, 4). "S then T": center (1, 2) → (2, 1) → (5, 1). The two results were different.
y-m-46-10.s.s1.st.1.after: The center of "T then S" is (2, 4) and the center of "S then T" is (5, 1), so they are different circles. A counterexample has appeared, so the statement "they are always the same" does not hold.
y-m-46-10.s.s1.st.1.r.c: The two centers come out different, (2, 4) and (5, 1). Redo the two calculations yourself.
y-m-46-10.s.s1.st.2.info:
We organized it with several T.
(a, b) | center of T then S | center of S then T | same?
(3, 3) | (5, 4) | (5, 4) | same
(3, 0) | (2, 4) | (5, 1) | different
(−2, −2) | (0, −1) | (0, −1) | same
(2, −5) | (−3, 3) | (4, −4) | different
y-m-46-10.s.s1.st.2.after: In "T then S" the center is (2 + b, 1 + a), and in "S then T" it is (2 + a, 1 + b), so they are the same only when 2 + b = 2 + a, that is, when a = b. Since S swaps the x-coordinate and the y-coordinate, if T is done first, the translation amounts a and b are swapped as well.
y-m-46-10.s.s1.st.2.r.a: In (3, 3) and (−2, −2), a is not 0 but the results were the same. Look at what value the same rows in the table have in common.
y-m-46-10.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Only when a = −b (when a and b have opposite signs)
y-m-46-10.s.s1.st.2.r.b: In the same rows of the table, the signs of a and b are the same. Look for what the same rows have in common.
y-m-46-10.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Only when a = b (when the two moving distances are equal)
y-m-46-10.s.s1.st.2.r.c: The rows that were the same have a = b, and the rows that were different have a ≠ b. If you follow the coordinates of the center, it is the condition for 2 + b and 2 + a to be equal, and for 1 + a and 1 + b to be equal.
y-m-46-10.s.s1.st.2.r.d: They were the same in (3, 3) and (−2, −2).
y-m-46-10.s.s1.reflect: In the first case (3, 3), the answer was "same," and then in the second case "different" came out. Look back at what was risky about generalizing from one case where they were the same, and at what the same rows and the different rows of the table have in common.

y-m-46-10.s.s2.model.0: If T is done first, the center becomes (1 + a, 2 + b), and since S swaps the x-coordinate and the y-coordinate, it becomes (2 + b, 1 + a). If S is done first, it becomes (2, 1), and then with T it becomes (2 + a, 1 + b). So if a ≠ b, the x-coordinates 2 + b and 2 + a differ, so the results differ.
y-m-46-10.s.s2.model.1: S swaps the x-coordinate and the y-coordinate, so if the translation is done first, the translation amounts a and b are swapped as well, and it is as if the center moved horizontally by b and vertically by a. If S is done first, it moves horizontally by a and vertically by b. So if a and b are different, the result depends on the order.
